finding.headline: At 57, the 401(k) catch-up limit rises at ages 60 to 63, so saving more is possible then.
details: The IRS says a higher catch-up limit of $11,750 applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 in these plans, instead of $8,500.
For 2027, the 401(k) limit is $25,500, and the IRA limit stays at $7,500.
Social Security benefits rise for each month you delay past full retirement age, and the increase stops at age 70. Sign up for Medicare at age 65 to avoid possible extra cost.

finding.headline: About 11% of your pay goes to tax now, and almost none in retirement.
details: Of your $22,000 pay, about $2,459 goes to tax today, and you keep about $19,541.
In retirement, the plan estimates only $3 a year in tax on withdrawals, so your tax share drops to about 0%.
Draw on taxable and cash savings first, then the 401(k) and IRA, and Roth savings last. This is a rough guide, not tax advice.

finding.headline: This household has no children, pets, or college costs, so family costs end.
details: Family costs are $0 this year and in total, so none of them carry into retirement.
Once retired, basic living costs are about $16,300 a year, or $1,358 a month.
Health costs before Medicare at age 65 are about $10,000 a year, and long-term care could cost $129,575 a year for about 3 years.

finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 95.
details: At age 95, there is about a 21% chance you are still alive, so the plan runs that far.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $659 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $14,400 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 69, which pays about $16,700 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 95. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
